posts.author: Ed Wesly
posts.content_md: I ran across a formula for a rehalogenating bleach based on potassium dichromate and potassium bromide, but instead of using sulfuric acid they are using *toluene-4-sulphonic acid*. Is there any advantage to using this stuff?

posts.author: Martin
posts.content_md:
> **Ed Wesly:** I ran across a formula for a rehalogenating bleach based on potassium dichromate and potassium bromide, but instead of using sulfuric acid they are usingtoluene-4-sulphonic acid. Is there any advantage to using this stuff?

Here's an excerpt from a mail I received from Jeff Blyth in 2004:

> I did investigate the effect of using milder acids in dichromate baths over 20 years ago and like you seem to have found, it can give noticeably better results. So one is restricted to finding alternatives which won't oxidise.One acid I got very nice results from is toluene 4-sulfonic acid. I put this in a paper in the Lake forest symposium of July 1985. Compared to this the hydrogensulfate is second best as it is still too strong ideally.

posts.author: Ed Wesly
posts.content_md: Thank you! Now the problem becomes where to get this stuff!

posts.author: Tom B.
posts.content_md: The really interesting question is (assuming there is a difference) - WHY are the results better? How could this be determined? It would really be nice to have a comparison at nanometer scale of the fringe structures and the resulting diffraction efficiencies for both recipes. Even without understanding, this suggests that some creative messing around with the very poorly understood dynamic chemistry involved in rehalogenated bleaching would be worthwhile.

Without really understanding the subtleties involved with bleaching, I gathered that highly acid bleaches tended to produce plenty of scatter (probably due to grain growth). Moreover, at low pH the gelatin may get damaged.

And regarding dichromate bleaches, pH control may be key in order to benefit from optimum crosslinking.

posts.author: Tom B.
posts.content_md: Could the difference be that the toluene stuff is non-oxidizing? The theory being that rehalogenation works better at low ph, and this stuff does less oxidative damage to the gelatin. The reason for wanting to elucidate this is that if oxidation is the problem, maybe anti-oxidant additives to conventional bleach (for example ascorbic acid ???) might be worth a try. I'm reminded of Brilland bleach which uses citric acid with FE3 and works pretty well - what would happen if some ascorbic acid was substituted? Sounds pretty silly to use a developing agent in a bleach, but who knows? Assuming that ascorbic really is an anti-oxidant under these conditions...

One of the main problems seems to be the oxidation of the acid.

For example, the citric acid you mentioned, won't remain stable with strong oxidizers like permanganate or dichromate (whereas it works with weaker oxidizers like ferric sulfate, copper sulfate).

I guess ascorbic acid cannot be used in this context.

Could we first please just get our terminology sorted or we are going to confuse ourselves and others.

The word Tom should have used was **"non-oxidable"** acid and not "non-oxidizing". 

Dichromate is itself an actual oxidizing acid as explained before here.

In water it breaks down into chromate ion (CrO4)-- and chromic acid (H2CrO4). 

I originally (around 1985) did some experiments to see if reducing the acidity of the DICHROMATE reversal

bleach actually improved the final image. The answer was that it did (using Agfa material then.) The improvement was not huge but worth pursuing. I first switched over to using the non nasty sodium hydrogen

sulfate instead of the generally used nasty sulfuric acid. I then tried other acids . Toluene sulfonic acid worked nicely, bleaching took longer though. (but you should'nt Hurry Holography ).

I found I could not wait for ever though by relying on the natural acidity of dichromate alone even ammonium dichromate. Acetic acid which is another non -oxidizable acid in the solution was simply not strong enough .

However please note now that there is no need to use p-toluene sulfonic acid , I have found that cutting down the sodium hydrogen sulfate to about 1% (or even 1/2 %)does the same job. I have put this on the Holowiki.

Jeff
